lesson.title: Rows and Columns With Meaning: What Periods and Groups Really Tell You
lesson.summary: The periodic table's rows (periods) and columns (groups) are not just a grid; each encodes real information about which electron shell is filling and which valence configuration an element has.
lesson.body:
Once elements are correctly ordered by atomic number, the periodic table's grid stops being arbitrary and starts encoding real information. Each horizontal row is called a period, and each vertical column is called a group, numbered 1 through 18 under modern conventions. Both dimensions of this grid trace directly back to how electrons fill an atom's orbitals, which is why elements that sit near each other on the table so often behave alike.

A period corresponds to the principal energy level, n, of the valence electrons being filled as you move across it. Period 1 has only two elements, hydrogen and helium, because there is nowhere to put electrons except the single 1s orbital. Period 2 has eight elements, lithium through neon, spanning the 2s and 2p orbitals. Period 3 again has eight elements, sodium through argon, filling 3s and 3p. Starting with period 4, rows get longer, eighteen elements each, because the d orbitals of one shell fill in alongside the s orbital of the next shell; periods 6 and 7 stretch to thirty-two elements once f orbitals join the mix. The length of each row is not decorative, it is a direct count of how many electrons fit into the orbitals becoming available at that energy level.

A group, by contrast, collects elements that share the same valence electron configuration pattern, which is why they tend to share chemical behavior too. Every alkali metal in group 1, lithium (1s2 2s1), sodium ([Ne]3s1), and potassium ([Ar]4s1) among them, has exactly one valence electron sitting alone in an s orbital. That shared setup is why they all react vigorously with water in essentially the same way, losing that lone electron to form a +1 ion: 2 Na(s) + 2 H2O(l) -> 2 NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Every halogen in group 17, fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine, instead has the configuration ns2 np5, one electron short of a filled octet, which is why they all tend to grab one extra electron and form -1 ions instead.

Because period tells you which shell is the valence shell and group tells you how many valence electrons occupy it, and in what pattern for main group elements, the two coordinates together pin down an atom's valence configuration almost completely. An element sitting in period 3, group 17 has no other option but to be chlorine, with the valence configuration 3s2 3p5: period 3 sets n = 3, and group 17 sets the s2p5 electron count. The periodic table is, in this sense, a coordinate system for electron configuration.

This is also why properties change smoothly and predictably as you move around the table rather than randomly. Moving down a group keeps the valence electron pattern the same while increasing n, adding a whole new shell each step. Moving across a period keeps n the same while steadily adding electrons and protons within that shell. Those two very different kinds of change produce two very different, very consistent trends in atomic size, ionization energy, and reactivity, which is exactly the subject of the next chapter, periodic trends.
